questions.question: What does ASG stand for in AWS?

options.text: Application Scaling Gateway
Auto Scaling Group
Automatic Server Group
Auto Server Gateway

explanation.correct: ASG stands for Auto Scaling Group — it manages a fleet of EC2 instances automatically.
explanation.why: A, C, D are all invented terms. Only Auto Scaling Group is correct.

questions.question: What are the three pieces of information you MUST provide when creating an Auto Scaling Group?

options.text: AMI ID, Key Pair, VPC
Launch Template, Size Limits, Scaling Policy
Instance Type, Region, Availability Zone
Security Group, Subnet, IAM Role

explanation.correct: ASG requires: a Launch Template (what to launch), Size Limits (min/desired/max), and a Scaling Policy (when to scale).
explanation.why: The other options are details inside the Launch Template, not the three top-level ASG requirements.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'Desired Capacity' in an Auto Scaling Group?

options.text: The maximum number of instances allowed
The minimum number of instances always running
The number of instances ASG tries to maintain at all times
The number of instances used for health checks

explanation.correct: Desired Capacity is the target number ASG tries to maintain. It starts with this count and adjusts based on scaling policies.
explanation.why: A is Maximum Size. B is Minimum Size. D is not a real ASG concept.

questions.question: Your ASG has Minimum 2, Desired 3, Maximum 6. Traffic drops to near zero. How many instances will be running?

explanation.correct: ASG will never scale below the Minimum Size, which is 2. Even with zero traffic, 2 instances remain.
explanation.why: A and B are below the minimum. D is the desired, but scaling in reduces below desired toward the minimum.

questions.question: What is horizontal scaling?

options.text: Upgrading the CPU and RAM of an existing server
Adding more servers to distribute load
Increasing the storage size of an instance
Moving servers between Availability Zones

explanation.correct: Horizontal scaling (scale out) means adding more instances. It eliminates single points of failure.
explanation.why: A is vertical scaling (scale up). C is storage expansion. D is migration, not scaling.

questions.question: What is a Launch Template used for in an ASG?

options.text: To define when to scale in or out
To set the minimum and maximum instance count
To provide the configuration blueprint for new instances ASG creates
To configure the load balancer listener rules

explanation.correct: A Launch Template defines the AMI, instance type, key pair, security groups, and user data — the blueprint for every new instance ASG launches.
explanation.why: A is the scaling policy. B is the size limits. D is an ALB configuration, not a Launch Template.

questions.question: Which load balancer operates at Layer 7 of the OSI model?

options.text: Classic Load Balancer (CLB)
Network Load Balancer (NLB)
Application Load Balancer (ALB)
Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB)

explanation.correct: ALB operates at Layer 7 (Application Layer) and understands HTTP/HTTPS traffic. This enables path-based and host-based routing.
explanation.why: NLB is Layer 4. GWLB is Layer 3. CLB operates at Layer 4 and 7 but is legacy.

questions.question: What is a Target Group in ALB?

options.text: A group of scaling policies
A logical grouping of targets (EC2, Lambda, IP) that ALB routes traffic to
A set of IAM permissions for the load balancer
A collection of ALB rules and listeners

explanation.correct: A Target Group holds the destinations (EC2 instances, Lambda, IPs) and manages health checks. ALB routes to healthy targets in the group.
explanation.why: A is an ASG concept. C is IAM, unrelated. D mixes up ALB components.

questions.question: What does an ALB Listener do?

options.text: Monitors EC2 CPU and triggers scaling
Checks connection requests on a specific port/protocol and routes based on rules
Sends health check requests to EC2 instances
Distributes traffic only to instances in the same AZ

explanation.correct: A Listener sits on a port (e.g., 80 for HTTP) and routes incoming traffic using defined rules to Target Groups.
explanation.why: A is CloudWatch/ASG. C is health checks (done by Target Group). D is not how listeners work.

questions.question: What happens when an ALB marks a target as unhealthy?

options.text: The target is terminated immediately
The ALB stops sending new traffic to that target until it passes health checks again
The ALB sends a notification to the user
The entire Target Group is deregistered

explanation.correct: ALB removes unhealthy targets from rotation — no new requests are sent to them. Existing connections drain. When health checks pass again, they're added back.
explanation.why: A is termination (done by ASG if ELB health check is enabled). C and D are not how ALB health checks work.

questions.question: What is path-based routing in ALB?

options.text: Routing based on the source IP address of the client
Routing based on the domain name in the Host header
Routing based on the URL path in the HTTP request
Routing based on the HTTP method (GET, POST)

explanation.correct: Path-based routing uses the URL path (e.g., /api vs /images) to forward traffic to different Target Groups.
explanation.why: B is host-based routing. A uses IP-based routing not in ALB rules. D is method-based routing, a different condition.

questions.question: Which scaling type is AWS recommended as the preferred policy for most production workloads?

options.text: Simple Scaling
Step Scaling
Manual Scaling
Target Tracking Scaling

explanation.correct: Target Tracking Scaling is AWS-recommended. It works like a thermostat — automatically adjusts capacity to maintain a target metric (e.g., 50% CPU).
explanation.why: Simple Scaling has cooldown limitations. Step requires manual threshold configuration. Manual scaling is not automated.

questions.question: A company wants to scale EC2 instances proactively before a predicted traffic spike every Monday morning. Which scaling type should they use?

options.text: Simple Scaling
Target Tracking Scaling
Predictive Scaling
Manual Scaling

explanation.correct: Predictive Scaling uses ML to analyze historical patterns and provisions capacity BEFORE the spike — ideal for recurring Monday morning traffic.
explanation.why: Simple and Target Tracking are reactive (after the spike starts). Manual requires human action.

questions.question: A company runs batch processing jobs every Sunday at 2 AM. The job finishes by 6 AM and requires 10 instances. The rest of the week, only 2 instances are needed. Which scaling policy is best?

options.text: Target Tracking Scaling
Step Scaling
Scheduled Scaling
Predictive Scaling

explanation.correct: Scheduled Scaling is perfect for known, time-based events. You define exactly when to scale up (Sunday 2 AM → 10 instances) and scale down (Sunday 6 AM → 2 instances).
explanation.why: Target Tracking and Step are reactive and don't know your schedule. Predictive uses ML and is less appropriate for already-known schedules.

questions.question: What is the key difference between Step Scaling and Simple Scaling?

options.text: Simple Scaling uses CloudWatch alarms; Step Scaling does not
Step Scaling can perform different actions based on the size of the alarm breach; Simple Scaling performs a fixed action
Simple Scaling is only for scale-in; Step Scaling is only for scale-out
Step Scaling has a cooldown period; Simple Scaling does not

explanation.correct: Step Scaling can add 1 instance at 60% CPU, 2 at 75%, and 3 at 90% — the response is proportional to the alarm breach size. Simple Scaling performs the same fixed action regardless.
explanation.why: Both use CloudWatch alarms. Both can scale in or out. Simple Scaling has the cooldown, not Step.

questions.question: When an ASG launches a new instance and it's attached to an ALB Target Group, what happens automatically?

options.text: The instance must be manually registered with the Target Group
The new instance is automatically registered with the Target Group and traffic is sent to it after health checks pass
The ALB restarts to recognize the new instance
The Target Group creates a new listener for the new instance

explanation.correct: ASG automatically registers new instances with the attached Target Group. Once health checks pass, ALB starts sending traffic — no manual action needed.
explanation.why: A is incorrect — registration is automatic when ASG is linked to a Target Group. C and D do not happen.

questions.question: What is the difference between EC2 health checks and ELB health checks in an ASG?

options.text: EC2 checks monitor CPU; ELB checks monitor memory
EC2 checks detect hardware/OS failures; ELB checks detect application-level failures
They are identical — both check the same things
ELB health checks are only for NLB, not ALB

explanation.correct: EC2 health checks detect infrastructure issues (instance not responding, status check failed). ELB health checks detect application failures (app returns 500, web server not running).
explanation.why: AWS recommends enabling ELB health checks so ASG replaces instances that fail at the application level, not just the OS level.

questions.question: An ALB receives requests for api.company.com and www.company.com. Both should be routed to different Target Groups. Which ALB feature enables this?

options.text: Path-based routing
Host-based routing
Weighted routing
Geographic routing

explanation.correct: Host-based routing uses the Host header (domain name) to route traffic to different Target Groups. api.company.com → API group; www.company.com → Web group.
explanation.why: Path-based routing uses the URL path (e.g., /api vs /web). Weighted and geographic routing are Route 53 features, not ALB.

questions.question: A security engineer says EC2 instances behind an ALB should NOT be directly accessible from the internet. How do you enforce this?

options.text: Disable public IPs on the instances
Set the EC2 security group to allow inbound traffic only from the ALB's security group
Use a private ALB instead of a public one
Disable the HTTP listener on the ALB

explanation.correct: Configure the EC2 instance security group to only allow inbound traffic from the ALB security group (not 0.0.0.0/0). This ensures traffic MUST flow through the ALB.
explanation.why: Disabling public IPs helps but isn't the complete control. A private ALB would affect external users. Disabling the listener breaks the app.

questions.question: What does 'Cross-Zone Load Balancing' mean in the context of ALB?

options.text: ALB can forward traffic across different AWS regions
Each ALB node distributes traffic evenly to all registered targets across all enabled AZs, not just its own AZ
ALB nodes can communicate with each other across AZs
Health checks are performed across multiple AZs simultaneously

explanation.correct: With Cross-Zone Load Balancing (enabled by default on ALB), each node can send traffic to any target in any AZ — not just the AZ it's in. This ensures even distribution.
explanation.why: ALB does not cross regions. The other options describe functionality that doesn't exist as described.

questions.question: An ASG is configured with Target Tracking Scaling at 50% CPU. There are 4 running instances averaging 80% CPU. How will ASG respond?

options.text: It will immediately terminate 2 instances to balance the load
It will add instances until the average CPU approaches 50%
It will wait for a CloudWatch alarm to manually trigger
It will increase the maximum size limit to allow more instances

explanation.correct: Target Tracking automatically calculates how many instances are needed to bring average CPU back to the 50% target and adds them. 4 instances at 80% CPU ≈ 6.4 instances needed to reach 50%, so it would add ~3 instances.
explanation.why: A is scale-in behavior (happens when CPU is too low). C is Simple/Step Scaling behavior. D never happens — ASG doesn't auto-modify max size.

questions.question: What is the minimum amount of historical data Predictive Scaling requires to generate forecasts?

options.text: 1 hour
12 hours
24 hours
7 days

explanation.correct: Predictive Scaling needs at least 24 hours of data to start making predictions. For best accuracy, AWS recommends 2 weeks of history.
explanation.why: 1 hour and 12 hours are too short. 7 days is the recommendation for GOOD accuracy, but 24 hours is the minimum to start.

questions.question: A company uses an ALB with three listeners: port 80 (HTTP), port 443 (HTTPS), and port 8080 (custom). A user hits the ALB on port 8081. What happens?

options.text: ALB forwards to the closest listener (port 8080)
ALB returns a connection refused error — no listener is configured on port 8081
ALB redirects to port 80
ALB forwards to the default Target Group

explanation.correct: If no listener is configured on port 8081, the ALB has nothing to accept the connection on that port. The request is dropped/refused.
explanation.why: ALB does not auto-route to nearby ports or default targets for unconfigured ports. Each port needs an explicit listener.

questions.question: You have an ASG with Desired 3, Min 1, Max 5. A Target Tracking policy targets 40% CPU. A Scheduled Scaling action fires and sets Desired Capacity to 5. The CPU across 5 instances drops to 10%. What does Target Tracking do?

options.text: Nothing — Scheduled actions take priority and Target Tracking is suspended
Target Tracking will scale in to bring CPU back toward 40%, but won't go below Min (1 instance)
Target Tracking will immediately override the scheduled action and set desired to 1
Target Tracking disables itself when Scheduled Scaling is active

explanation.correct: Both policies can coexist. After the Scheduled action sets desired to 5, Target Tracking may scale in since CPU is only 10%. It will remove instances until CPU approaches 40%, but never below the Minimum of 1.
explanation.why: Target Tracking doesn't suspend for Scheduled. It doesn't immediately go to 1 — it scales in gradually toward the target metric.

questions.question: An ALB rule has multiple conditions. Which is a valid ALB rule condition type?

options.text: CPU utilization
Host header, Path pattern, HTTP header, Query string, Source IP
Instance health status
Number of registered targets

explanation.correct: ALB rules support conditions on: Host header, Path pattern, HTTP header, HTTP method, Query string, and Source IP. These are all Layer 7 (application-level) attributes.
explanation.why: CPU is a CloudWatch metric (ASG concern). Health status and target count are Target Group metrics, not routing conditions.

questions.question: A company needs to perform a blue/green deployment using ALB. What is the correct approach?

options.text: Create two ALBs — one for blue, one for green — and use Route 53 to switch between them
Use one ALB with two Target Groups (blue and green). Update the listener rule weight to gradually shift traffic from blue to green
Terminate the blue ASG and launch a green ASG with a new ALB
Use two separate VPCs — one for blue, one for green

explanation.correct: ALB supports weighted routing between Target Groups on a listener rule. You can gradually shift traffic from blue (100%) to green (0%) in increments until green takes full traffic — all with zero downtime.
explanation.why: Option A wastes resources and has DNS propagation delays. C causes downtime. D is unnecessarily complex.

questions.question: What happens to an EC2 instance when ASG decides to scale in (terminate it), and that instance is registered with an ALB Target Group?

options.text: ASG terminates the instance immediately, then the Target Group removes it
ASG sends a termination signal; the instance is first deregistered from the Target Group (connection draining), then terminated
The ALB must be restarted after the instance is terminated
The Target Group removes the instance only after the next health check interval

explanation.correct: ASG puts the instance into a 'Terminating:Wait' lifecycle state. Connection draining allows existing requests to complete. Once drained (or timeout), the instance is deregistered and then terminated.
explanation.why: Immediate termination (A) would drop active connections. C is false — ALB doesn't restart. D is not how deregistration works.

questions.question: Which ALB feature allows you to route traffic between microservices where each service has a different URL path — all behind the same domain?

options.text: Health checks
Sticky sessions
Path-based routing using listener rules
Cross-zone load balancing

explanation.correct: Path-based routing with ALB listener rules lets you route /api → API service, /auth → Auth service, /images → Media service — all under one domain, one ALB.
explanation.why: Health checks are for availability. Sticky sessions maintain user affinity to one instance. Cross-zone is about AZ distribution, not URL-based routing.

questions.question: An exam asks: 'A company's web application needs to serve millions of TCP connections per second with ultra-low latency. Which load balancer?' What is the correct answer?

options.text: Application Load Balancer
Classic Load Balancer
Network Load Balancer
Gateway Load Balancer

explanation.correct: NLB (Network Load Balancer) operates at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) and is designed for extreme performance — millions of requests per second with microsecond latency.
explanation.why: ALB is Layer 7 and adds HTTP parsing overhead (great for web routing, not for raw TCP performance). CLB is legacy. GWLB is for security appliances.

questions.question: An ASG is set up with ELB health checks enabled. An EC2 instance passes all EC2 status checks but the Apache web server process has crashed. What happens?

options.text: Nothing — EC2 status checks pass, so the instance is considered healthy
ASG marks the instance unhealthy based on ELB health checks and replaces it with a new instance
The ALB continues sending traffic to the instance until the user manually terminates it
ASG waits for the EC2 status check to fail before taking action

explanation.correct: ELB health checks test at the application level (HTTP requests to a path). If Apache is down, the HTTP health check fails, ALB marks the instance unhealthy, ASG gets the signal and terminates + replaces it — even though EC2 OS-level checks pass.
explanation.why: This is exactly why enabling ELB health checks on ASG (not just EC2) is a best practice. EC2 checks only catch hardware/OS failures.

questions.question: What is 'Connection Draining' (also called Deregistration Delay) in ALB?

options.text: A process that blocks new requests during ALB maintenance
The time ALB waits for in-flight requests to complete before deregistering a target
A technique to drain excess traffic from overloaded instances
The process of removing unused listeners from ALB

explanation.correct: Connection Draining (Deregistration Delay) gives in-flight requests time to complete (default 300 seconds) when a target is deregistered — either by ASG scale-in or manual removal. After the delay, the target is fully removed.
explanation.why: It ensures no active user requests are dropped during scale-in or deployments.

questions.question: A startup wants the simplest way to ensure their EC2 fleet always uses exactly 50% CPU. They don't want to manage alarm thresholds. Which ASG policy fits best?

options.text: Step Scaling with three alarm levels
Simple Scaling with a single CloudWatch alarm
Target Tracking Scaling with Average CPU Utilization at 50%
Scheduled Scaling with hourly adjustments

explanation.correct: Target Tracking with CPU target 50% is the simplest approach — you set the target and AWS manages everything else. No alarms, no steps, no manual configuration needed.
explanation.why: Step and Simple scaling require manual CloudWatch alarm setup. Scheduled scaling requires known patterns and manual hour-by-hour setup.

questions.question: Which protocol does ALB NOT support?

options.text: HTTP
HTTPS
WebSocket
UDP

explanation.correct: ALB supports HTTP, HTTPS, and WebSocket (Layer 7 protocols). UDP is a Layer 4 protocol supported by NLB, not ALB.
explanation.why: For UDP traffic, use Network Load Balancer.

questions.question: In a two-tier architecture, a Public Load Balancer receives traffic on port 80 and forwards to a Web Tier Subnet. The web servers then communicate with backend servers through an Internal Load Balancer on port 443. What type of architecture is this?

options.text: Single-tier flat architecture
Multi-tier architecture with public and internal load balancers
Serverless architecture
Peer-to-peer architecture

explanation.correct: This is a classic multi-tier architecture — a public ALB faces the internet on port 80, and an internal ALB handles backend-to-database tier communication on port 443 (HTTPS internally).
explanation.why: This pattern is very common in production and appeared in the session's diagram showing Web Tier and Business Tier subnets.

questions.question: What does 'Single Point of Failure' (SPOF) mean in the context of vertical scaling?

options.text: Only one person manages the server
If the one server fails, the entire application goes down
The server can only run one application at a time
The server has only one network interface

explanation.correct: A Single Point of Failure (SPOF) is a component that, if it fails, brings down the whole system. Vertical scaling still uses one server — if it fails, everything stops.
explanation.why: Horizontal scaling (multiple instances) eliminates SPOF. This is why AWS recommends horizontal scaling over vertical for critical workloads.

questions.question: ASG is in a VPC with subnets in three Availability Zones. What is the benefit of distributing instances across multiple AZs?

options.text: Instances in multiple AZs have better CPU performance
If one AZ experiences an outage, instances in other AZs continue serving traffic
Multiple AZs reduce the cost of EC2 instances
Only instances in multiple AZs can use Launch Templates

explanation.correct: Deploying across multiple AZs provides high availability. If one AZ goes down (power outage, hardware failure), ASG and ALB automatically route traffic only to healthy instances in the remaining AZs.
explanation.why: AZ distribution doesn't affect CPU, cost, or Launch Template eligibility — it provides fault tolerance.

questions.question: Which of the following is TRUE about a Classic Load Balancer (CLB)?

options.text: CLB is the newest and most feature-rich load balancer
CLB is a legacy product and AWS recommends using ALB or NLB for new applications
CLB only supports HTTPS traffic
CLB operates at Layer 7 only

explanation.correct: Classic Load Balancer is the original ELB and is now considered legacy. AWS recommends ALB for HTTP/HTTPS and NLB for TCP/UDP for all new applications.
explanation.why: CLB is the oldest, not newest. It supports both Layer 4 and 7. There's no HTTPS-only restriction.

questions.question: What is the default health check path for ALB Target Groups?

options.text: /health
/status
/check

explanation.correct: The default health check path is / (root). ALB sends an HTTP GET to / and expects a 2xx or 3xx response. You can customize this to any path like /health.
explanation.why: AWS default is / — you can change it to /health or /ping, but the default out-of-the-box is always /.

questions.question: An engineer wants to keep costs low during off-peak hours while ensuring minimum service availability. They set ASG Minimum=2, Desired=5, Maximum=10. During off-peak, CPU stays at 5%. What will Target Tracking do?

options.text: Keep running all 10 instances
Terminate all instances since CPU is very low
Scale in toward Minimum, maintaining at least 2 instances
Increase Desired Capacity to match the minimum

explanation.correct: Target Tracking scales in when metric is below target, removing instances gradually. It will never go below Minimum (2). So it scales from 5 → 4 → 3 → 2 and stops there.
explanation.why: It can never go below Minimum regardless of how low traffic is. 10 instances are the max, not the current state.

questions.question: An ALB has a listener on port 80 with two rules: Rule 1 (priority 1): path=/api/* → Target Group A. Rule 2 (priority 2, default): ALL traffic → Target Group B. A request arrives for /api/users. Where does it go?

options.text: Target Group B — default rule always takes precedence
Both Target Group A and B
Target Group A — highest priority matching rule wins
The request is rejected — two rules conflict

explanation.correct: ALB evaluates rules in priority order (lowest number = highest priority). Rule 1 matches /api/*, so the request goes to Target Group A. The default rule is only reached if no other rule matches.
explanation.why: Default rule is a catch-all, not a highest priority. Rules do not conflict — they're evaluated in order and the first match wins.
